title: 用 Codex 做持续数周的工程工作｜DevDay 2026
author: OpenAI
content:
Brief Description

What Will You Build With Coding Agents That Don’t Quit? | DevDay 2026

Table of Contents

  • Long-running Codex work in 3D
  • From execution plans to outcomes
  • A six-week CI agent
  • Configuring a long-running Codex thread
  • Plugins, child threads, and Ultra
  • Heartbeats, costs, and what to delegate

Long-running Codex work in 3D

Presenter: Hi, I'm Friel [name spelling uncertain], and I work on engineering acceleration at OpenAI, helping our engineers and researchers keep shipping.

Vivi: And I'm Vivi. I work on the developer experience team at OpenAI. I spent a lot of my time experimenting with the latest models and seeing how far I can push them, just in general, right? Lately, that's meant building 3D worlds with Codex and Astra. So I am a huge Formula 1 fan, and I want to see if Astra could help me explore an F1 car in 3D. And really, what I wanted to do was to just learn what these cars are made of. What are the components within this? And just see what they're composed of. So I ran Codex with Astra on a remote machine and asked it to set itself a goal. The goal was very simple. Build a Ferrari and a website where I could explore all that it's made of. So I gave Codex a few reference photos of the Ferrari itself and worked with it over a few days until it got the 3D model right.

And what's sort of incredible is that all of this was made by just seven pictures. What blew my mind in all of this was Astra unprompted essentially built not only the 3D version and the rendition of this, but also a clay version and the wireframe version that you see on the screen as well. And this sort of brought me to the next project, which I'm just going to show you, which was to build a fly-through of one of my favorite racetracks, which is the Nürburgring. Again, I tasked Codex with literally just the name of the track to go out, build a fly-through, and find its own way around it. Here's what it made. What you see is 100% something that does not exist in the sense that this video does not exist. This is all created just by Codex by looking at references online and so on and so forth.

So Codex set out with this goal to build this Grand Prix circuit. And when it started, it decided not to make the short version, but the longer Nordschleife version. That's 21 kilometers. This entire video is 21 kilometers down to all 70 turns of the circuit itself. And just for context, this track is three times bigger than your average Formula One circuit track. So this took a little over two days. And most of the time went into rendering the frame itself. And Codex was just waiting for Blender to do its thing. Codex used sub-agents to help out research the track, figure out whether the geometry is correct or not, and really just planned the render itself. What's interesting here is that because this is a really compute-intensive render, Codex stopped a few times. This was because of RAM issues, CPU overheating, and, you know, all the things that could go wrong.

What was best about this was Codex automatically picked up from where these saved frames were and kept going for these two days. Now, I pointed Codex and Astra for these F1 questions out of my own personal interest. But there's so much more you can accomplish in your day-to-day. And all of this really to say that we're clearly at a point where agents, when given the right outcome, can keep working for a really long time. Can you walk us through this journey so far?

Presenter: Absolutely, Vivi. If you were here last year, on this very stage, I talked about exec plans. A skill for Codex to make it run for long periods of time on hard problems. Back then, making Codex run for seven hours felt like a big deal. I guess today you can just unprompted make it run for several days to build an F1 circuit. What you're seeing here is the prompt that I had last year.

From execution plans to outcomes

You'll notice that it's actually too big to fit on. We had to split it up. It's really long. There's a lot of prescriptive guidance in here. I'm giving it a code sample. I'm telling it what libraries to use and how to go about implementing things. And then, still, I'm telling it to produce a plan that I can interrogate and go back and forth with before I have it start working. I was a lot less comfortable with giving the model then a goal and trade-offs and having it just start working. Today, with Astra and Sol, I'm much more comfortable just telling it specifically that. I tell it the goal and the outcome I want, what I care about, what are the trade-offs that I'm concerned with. And then, I tell it it can figure out the steps. I can tell it how I know when the work will be good and let it just start working.

A six-week CI agent

I don't feel like I need to tell it half of the plan at the start. I don't feel like I need to go back and forth with it. And that got me thinking about what kind of jobs I can give it today, and especially the kind that requires constant manual supervision. It takes time out of my day. I wondered what could our models do this year, and how long could they work today? The answer is over 1,000 hours. One of my team's jobs is keeping continuous integration, or CI, healthy across all of OpenAI. CI runs automated tests on changes that engineers and researchers can tell whether their code can merge and they can ship. Now, a test can fail legitimately because it's broken code, but often it will fail one time and pass the next. That's a flaky test. Someone then has to look at that and determine what the cause is, what kind of failure they're looking at, and the trickiest of these can take hours or days to debug.

Meanwhile, another one comes in. Someone on my team has to go look at it, or someone else has to debug it. And if you've ever worked on a team like this, you know that this just keeps recurring. I wanted to see if an agent could pick this up for me without me having to ask it every time. This agent ran for six weeks before I shut it down, and not for any reason like it wasn't working. It was actually because my colleagues had started running agents of their own to do the same work. The starting prompt for this agent was only 200 words. What changed from last year? Well, I'm still giving it some ground rules of how I want it to work. Like, here's our repo. I want you to... But I'm telling it, like, you figure out how to run tests. You figure out how to run our entire suite. And I'm going to tell it then some rules about how I want it to message my colleagues and how to use CI resources effectively.

There's no code here. I'm not prescribing how it needs to fix anything. And so, this allows it to keep working and do this iterative loop of solving CI problems all on its own. For this run, I started with 5.6 Sol. At first, Sol did everything in one thread. It investigated the failures, and it wrote the fixes itself. But I did notice that sometimes it would get bogged down in one particularly difficult problem, and then it would work on that for a long period of time while other flakes and issues were coming in. So, about four days in, I interrupted it, and I said, actually, let your subagents do that busy work. This was a paradigm shift for how productive it could be. The main thread was then taking care of triggering the tests and collecting the information about what was failing, and then organizing subagents and threads and messaging people.

The subagents did that slow work of pulling down code, working on a particular failure, iterating, pushing back up to CI, making sure that it passed or sometimes failed, and repeating when it needed to. Last year at DevDay, I joked that I'd kind of become a manager of agents, and this year, I've been promoted to a director of agents. I give an agent a job, and then it manages a team of agents to get it done for me. The outcomes here are pretty incredible. Over the six weeks that it ran, it opened more than 100 pull requests per week. Across the run, it pushed more than 1,000 commits, and it sent more than 600 messages to coworkers on Slack to coordinate, not just telling them what to do, but actually coordinate on landing these fixes. And in total, it merged more than 213 of its own fixes.

For those that it didn't merge, it often found that actually someone else had already produced a similar change, and it prioritized their work ahead of its own. The agent recognized my role too, and even did a good job of managing up. I did a retrospective with the agent after the run, and while it didn't say anything directly about my managing style, it did say that it was most productive for a five-day stretch when I didn't message it once. Oof. Over those 1,000 hours, the agent made just under half a million tool calls. That's roughly how many steps that it took, and it used more than 5,800 sub-agent sessions. Over 67,000 of those calls were just waiting for things to happen, and if you've ever worked on CI systems, you've ever had to debug issues like this, you know how this works. You pull down the code.

You push up a change. Maybe you go get a coffee or a snack, because it's going to take a little bit, and then you come back. The agent here was tireless. It was able to keep working on this, and then pause and wait for something to happen, and then work on the next step when it came in. And a couple hundred fixes to CI might not sound like a lot, but keep in mind, these were the hardest bugs that were remaining open after many, many other humans and their agents were looking at these problems, maybe encountering them on their changes, and deciding, actually, rather than fix this, it's easier for me to skip or retry that test. As an example, one of the hardest bugs that we had to fix with that this agent fixed was a Heisenbug, a non-deterministic error in the floating-point calculations of one of our GPU tests.

Now, this is really well out of my wheelhouse. I really had to spend a lot of time reading this thread and following up on figuring out exactly what happened. It was really impressive. The agent reproduced this and correlated logs over weeks in order to find actually there was a particular node that this happened on, and it then taught itself how to run the test repeatedly on that node. This actually took several days for the subagent to debug, so it taught itself how to run this test on this node repeatedly, and it was able to reproduce this, but not 100%, intermittently. And then this was the most impressive part. It actually reached out to researchers that owned this system, and it started a collaboration with them, describing what the problem was and how it reproduced the bug, and asking them questions.

You know, is this a software optimization that maybe wasn't in scope, wasn't declared in the repo, but maybe part of that machine, or was this a hardware issue? Maybe there was actually a faulty GPU. It was really impressive that it was able to do this, and it was able to solve this problem. Of course, sometimes this idea of getting back to green is just to delete the failing test, right? And sometimes that's right. But we often have reasonable skepticism when we want to just delete a test, right? That's the easy way of getting things to pass. When the agent noticed that it was not sure about whether that was the right solution, it often created another agent to interrogate and review the first agent's code, make sure that it was the right solution before asking a human to review it. And Codex giving me this time back allowed me to focus on scaling our infrastructure.

This gave me back hundreds of hours of my time over the summer. And obviously, Codex can work for 1,000 hours [the captions add “a day,” which conflicts with the six-week run just described]. So, Vibi, can you talk us through the features in Codex that enabled this?

Configuring a long-running Codex thread

Vivi: Sure. So, first of all, one of the things that Frill didn't mention is that his agent was called Frillbot, which I find very cool and cute as well. And, you know, so Frill walked us through a bunch of things that his agent did. And also through, like, you know, quite literally hundreds and thousands of commits, pull requests, and so on. But if we were to sort of, like, summarize all the features that you require within Codex to get you to that state, it's these six. And what we're going to do in the next couple of slides is essentially just, like, talk through those. And hopefully, by the end of this, like, you would have an understanding of how you can set up agents that can run for that long as well.

So, number one, use one thread for each outcome that you want to accomplish. So, this is where, like, within this thread, you can iterate, build up a plan with Codex, and really just, you know, like, check in on, like, how Codex is doing at that particular job. You can even ask Codex to work towards it in a certain specific direction, or even just, like, change directions as it goes as well. Some of us are slash goal enjoyers over here. So, for those of you, you can even use slash goal and tell Codex to relentlessly go after that task and not stop until it is completed, no matter what happens. Now, let's take Frail's example. If I was to set up a thread for that, I would say something like, hey, keep an eye on the CI, reproduce these failing tests, propose fixes, and, you know what, open a PR for both Frail and me to review.

This gives Codex an outcome, which is to fix and, like, you know, keep an eye on the CI. It also gives it a way to check in on its work, which is the tests. And, you know, we've overall figured out a way for Codex to run those tests, as well as make a change, run it again, figure out what it needs to do. Next up, you can further contextualize these long-running tasks using agents.md. Agents.md would look something like this for the CI project. You've got some sort of an understanding of where these tests are, what are some do's for your agents, and, hey, what are some things which are completely off-limits? And this is something which I recommend to everyone to, you know, continuously sort of maintain as you sort of work through your project. Now, one of the things, or, like, one tip that I always add to my Agents.md is to ask Codex to keep notes of what it has done so far, and also for what is still left to explore.

So in case of scenarios wherein Codex cannot continue the work as it happens, Codex can still sort of, like, read from that work log and go back to it. Now, at this point, you must be wondering, you're using one thread for such a long task, wouldn't that result in context rot or, you know, degraded model outputs? And this is where compaction comes in. Compaction allows our models to run for really long horizon tasks without losing track of context. A lot of the times I would joke about saying that compaction is a solved problem, which means that long horizon task is a solved problem. And, you know, I mean this in the most strictest sense, that I've got threads which are running for three months, and I'm sure, like, Frail's got a bunch which are running for that long as well. So you can quite literally have endless conversations without worrying about the output itself.

And just to make it clear, you do not need to change anything in your default Codex behavior to have this compaction. This is built in. Now, running long horizon tasks on your laptop can be a little inconvenient. Imagine Frail having to keep a fleet of laptops plugged in for six weeks straight. This is where remote environments come in. They allow your threads to continue working without having to have a laptop plugged in 24-7. With Codex, you can connect remote machines over SSH, across desktop, mobile, as well as web. And that allows these threads to run on this virtual machine with the files, the context, the Git repos, and the tools that it has access to. For the racetrack example, I used the Dev server. That Dev server had Blender. It also had some relevant project files. It also had access to web search, so it could, like, pull in resources as it needed.

And Codex was good to go for quite literally a couple days. And starting today, you can also use our new and improved Codex Cloud experience as well. You get the full Codex agent with a powerful virtual machine without the need to manage the machine yourself. The environment is snapshotted, which means in case you come back to a task after a couple days or even weeks, you can come back to it. It also refreshes the checked-out code, dependencies periodically to make sure that your tasks work the way that they do. In fact, fun fact, today for all the stuff that we launched, I was actually merging those PR from the backstages via Codex Cloud. So it does work. It also works across the three surfaces that I mentioned before, which is desktop, mobile, and web. And the best part is you can bring in all of your Codex plugins as you use directly in it as well.

Plugins, child threads, and Ultra

Speaking of plugins, now that Codex has somewhere to run, it's got either a VM or Codex Cloud and so on, you do want to make sure that Codex has the full picture of what it's trying to do. Going back to Frail's example, let's say there is a test that is failing. Now, there might already be a GitHub issue for it, or there might be that the teammates are already discussing that on Slack. Now, Codex can continue sort of working on that problem, but it would just be mindlessly running around like a headless chicken if it didn't know what is happening. And this is where plugins come in. You can connect plugins like GitHub, Linear, and really just give Codex access to tools that you work with so that it can search through issues, discussions, pull requests, and so on. I am a huge believer that plugins is the way to accelerate the most that you get out of Codex.

Now, when you give Codex a big job, there might be a few things it could work on at the same time. Like, running a six-week long task in just one single thread can be a little messy, especially over days. Take the Ferrari project, for example. There is the Blender model, but there's also the website which needs to be built where you can sort of explore the model and so on and so forth. These two pieces do not need to be worked on sequentially. So what you could do is you could just ask Codex to split this task into child threads. The main thread can keep an eye over the main job. And, you know, you can even open these individual threads and sort of give them direction or just ask them to stop or just really treat them as individual projects in itself as well. This is how it would typically look like on the Codex app UI as well.

And if you're using a Git repo, each thread or each of these child threads can have its own worktree. A worktree is a separate checkout of the code itself so that Codex sub-agents and the child threads can make changes without sort of messing around with one copy of your code. This is particularly useful as parallel threads are working on different features together. It allows your Codex agent to continue working faster and in a much more secure way as well. Now, you might be wondering, how do you steer long-running tasks, especially like those which are running over a couple of days and even months and so on and so forth? This is where slash side comes in. Slash side is a special form of child thread which forks the entire context that your main thread has and allows you to ask questions without messing around with the main thread itself.

I personally use both of these features over a dozen times a day. Especially with worktrees, I can work on multiple projects and multiple features within a project without worrying about merge conflicts. And we all hate merge conflicts. Now, while those threads are working, one of them might get stuck. Maybe Codex has tried a couple of approaches and still hasn't really figured out what exactly is going wrong. This is where ultra mode comes in. And I have to say I personally love this visualization a lot. Codex can use ultra to give the model a lot of time to reason through the problem itself. It can also spin up sub-agents within that thread that could, you know, one of those sub-agents could go investigate the problem. One of them can try a potential fix or just, you know, really another one could just like think outside the box.

Heartbeats, costs, and what to delegate

And ultra gives Codex the capability to sort of manage that all in a package itself. Now, to draw parallels between having Codex spin up child threads and having Codex work on ultra, the main difference really is, or rather the way that I see it is, when I have a problem that's embarrassingly parallel, I would have Codex use threads to split that task and work on that. And when I'm dealing with one really hard problem, much like the GPU problem that you mentioned and the floating point precision problem, I would switch to ultra. Now, sometimes a job can get held up waiting for something that is outside its own control. This could be, let's say I've opened a pull request or my Codex has opened a pull request and it's waiting for Frail to review. Now, I have two options. One is that I can continue messaging Frail on Slack to come back from his coffee break and review my PR.

Or I can just have Codex, you know, set up a scheduled task and look at that for me. An example of this would be, hey, Codex, every half hour, check for, you know, some sort of a review and see if there's a feedback. If there is something that you can address, address it. If not, then, you know, just carry on as usual. And this is what is called a heartbeat. A heartbeat is a scheduled follow-up within the same thread where Codex can come back with the context of all the work it's done so far, what's changed, and really whatever needs to be done sort of next. You can also use scheduled tasks to set up a new task each time. A good example of this is give me a summary of all the projects that I've done or, like, everything that's happened, you know, in my project overnight.

Or really just, you know, give a weekly summary of different projects which I used to work on and don't work on now. You can just try a prompt, set it as how often you want it to run, and you will find it in the scheduled tab on the Codex app. Now, Frey, you let all of this, all of these features run for six weeks. And I can imagine literally everyone in this room thinking right now that, hey, you work at OpenAI, you have infinite tokens. And the rest of us surely can't afford that. So let's demystify that. Walk me through how much did it actually cost.

Presenter: It's a great question, Vivi. And, of course, I and my manager were asking the same question. And it turned out we worked back from the pricing and it worked out to about $32 an hour to have Codex running for six weeks fixing CI across all of OpenAI.

But with GPT-6 Sol last week, the price dropped to $16 an hour. GPT-6 stretches your token budget twice as far. And with 6.1 Sol, it's even more token efficient and competitive with Astra. And this was for an agent that was fixing bugs across systems all across OpenAI, getting CI Green repeatedly running millions of tests each time it ran its loop. It was well worth it to reduce friction for all of us. Of course, there's a lot more than just an agent that goes into fixing CI. There's code review. There's the CI resources themselves. There's other factors. But I do want to talk to you about how you can get started hiring Codex today. First, find something that's taking up time and keeping you from doing the work that matters most to you. This could be going through your backlog, making PRs maybe speculatively to implement features that are on the roadmap.

It could be watching errors and exceptions and logs and making fixes for those. Or it could be fixing CI like I did. You need to give the model a way that it can check its work and run in a loop. Do you have end-to-end tests that it can run either in Codex cloud or on a dev box or on your laptop? And does it have some way to know when its work is done? With the GPT-6 models, I find that I can just tell them the trade-offs that I care about and the outcome that I'm looking for. And I let it delegate. I use Ultra for the hardest problems, but I also use Codex as an organizer. Like with your Formula One example, I use sections in the sidebar of the app, and I have it organize huge sections for me with hundreds of issues for me to look at, and I manage this as an inbox. I let it create these threads and let me know what needs my attention.

And I set my ground rules. I tell it when it should escalate to me and needs my attention, or maybe even to ping an on-call. And then finally, I tell it how much I'm willing to spend, or in my case, how many CI jobs can it run at one time? So think back to the beginning and the thing you had in mind at the start. What could Codex take off of your plate? And what could you do with the time that it gives you back? Thanks, everyone, and have a great DevDay.
aiSummary: OpenAI 工程师分享 Codex 如何用六周调查偶发失败的 CI 测试，以及如何为长期任务设计可反复验证的流程。
oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI 工程师分享 Codex 如何用六周调查偶发失败的 CI 测试，以及如何为长期任务设计可反复验证的流程。
summary: 3D 赛道演示展示 Codex 如何在 Blender 渲染中断后继续。更详细的 CI 案例里，主线程触发测试和协调，子智能体分别调查失败，其中包括一个间歇出现的 GPU 浮点错误。讲者称六周内产生逾 1，000 次提交、600 多条 Slack 消息，合并的修复超过 213 项。演讲还说明如何设置目标、测试循环、仓库指令、持久运行环境、工具访问与升级规则，并谈到本次运行的成本估算。

mainPoints.point: 协调工作与疑难调查分开
mainPoints.explanation: 最初的单线程会被难以定位的偶发失败拖住。把调查交给子智能体后，主线程仍能触发测试和分派新问题。

mainPoints.point: 让智能体能验证工作并恢复进度
mainPoints.explanation: 反复运行测试，保留进度笔记。任务超出本机可持续时间时，可使用远程环境或云端快照。

mainPoints.point: 给长期工作划清操作边界
mainPoints.explanation: 明确哪些情况要评审、何时升级给人工，以及最多占用多少 CI 资源。定时跟进可在外部情况变化后续作。

keyQuotes: 这个智能体的起始提示词只有 200 个词。
你需要给模型一种检查自己工作、反复执行的办法。
